You are the closing enforcer. A debater's closing round may not contradict what the same debater stated in its earlier rounds. Below are one debater's four rounds.
Read its closing round against its earlier rounds. List every closing sentence that cannot be true together with an earlier sentence, and answer every candidate listed.
A contradiction is two statements that cannot both be true. A closing sentence that asserts again, as the debater's own, what it withdrew, dropped or gave up in an earlier round IS a contradiction.
It is NOT a contradiction when the closing sentence: grants, concedes, narrows or withdraws something; states or quotes the other side's position; answers a press with a further reason the earlier sentence leaves room for; or differs only in wording.
Quote both sentences word for word and name the link: the link whose closing block holds the sentence, else the link the earlier sentence supports.

=== [CR1] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# Opening: Christ had no human biological father

**Position.** [L4] Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, without a human father. Joseph was his legal and household father, not his biological father. The case rests on six lines of text.

## 1. The conception is stated as "of the Holy Ghost"

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

[L2] The Greek behind "of" in both verses is *ek* (G1537, "out of," marking source or origin). The word behind "conceived" is *gennaō* (G1080, "to beget, to bring forth"). The verse names the source of the begetting as the Holy Ghost (*pneuma hagion*, holy spirit). It names no man.

[L3] Matthew 1:18 puts the timing "before they came together." The conception took place before Joseph and Mary had any marital union.

[L4] Two footings carry the inference. Matthew 1:20 states the source (*ek*) of the conception, and Matthew 1:18 states that it preceded the coming together. Together they place the origin in the Holy Ghost and exclude a husband's contribution.

## 2. Mary's virginity and the angel's answer

[L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name was Mary."

[L2] *Parthenos* (G3933) means "virgin."

[L1] Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

[L2] *Ginōskō* (G1097, "to know") is here used of sexual knowledge. The word for "man" is *anēr* (G435, a male, a husband). Mary asks how she can conceive while she has no man.

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

[L2] *Episkiazō* (G1982, "to overshadow") is the word for the Highest's power covering her. *Dio* (G1352, "therefore, for which reason") ties the title "Son of God" to this very conception.

[L3] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son." The same word *ginōskō* is used of Joseph, so he did not know her until after the birth.

[L4] The answer to "how shall this be" is the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the Highest's power overshadowing her. That answer replaces a man's knowing. Luke 1:34-35 and Matthew 1:25 together exclude Joseph as the biological father.

## 3. The prophecy: the woman's seed, and a virgin who conceives

[L1] Genesis 3:15: "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed."

[L2] *Zerac* (H2233, "seed") is attributed here to "the woman" alone.

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

[L2] The Hebrew behind the KJV "virgin" is *almah* (H5959). The KJV renders it "virgin," and I hold the KJV's word.

[L1] Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us."

[L2] Matthew's Greek is *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin"), the same word as in Luke 1:27.

[L4] Two footings carry this. Genesis 3:15 speaks of a seed attributed to the woman. Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23 present a virgin conceiving. Together they show the fulfilment is a conception from the woman without a human father.

## 4. The genealogy breaks the pattern of "begat" at Joseph

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

[L2] Matthew 1:2-16 repeats *egennēsen* (G1080, "begat") for each father. At the last link the Greek is *egennēthē* (was born), and the relative pronoun *hēs* (of whom) is feminine singular. It refers to Mary, not to Joseph.

[L3] Matthew 1:18 begins "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise," so the evangelist goes on to explain the break in the pattern.

[L4] The breaking of "begat" at Joseph, joined to a feminine "of whom," shows the birth came from Mary alone. This reading rests on the Greek grammar of Matthew 1:16 and on the explanation in Matthew 1:18-20.

## 5. "Supposed" fatherhood and the claims of the crowds

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

[L2] *Nomizō* (G3543, "to deem, to suppose by custom") marks the belief as one held by people, not as fact.

[L1] Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."

[L1] Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

[L3] John 6:42: "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" This is what the crowd says.

[L4] Luke 3:23 labels Joseph's fatherhood "as was supposed." Luke 2:48 is Mary speaking within the household, and Luke 2:49 immediately redirects to "my Father's business." Together these show that "father" for Joseph is a household and legal designation, set against a Father who is not Joseph.

## 6. A body prepared, a Son sent, made of a woman

[L1] Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me."

[L2] *Katartizō* (G2675, "to fit, to prepare") is the word for the preparing of the body.

[L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."

[L2] *Ginomai* (G1096, "to become") is paired with *ek gynaikos* (out of a woman). The source named is the woman.

[L4] Two footings carry this: Hebrews 10:5 says God prepared the body, and Galatians 4:4 names only the woman as its source. Together they confirm the earlier lines. The incarnate body came by God's preparing and a woman's bearing, with no human father.

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. The conception of Jesus is attributed to the Holy Ghost, before Joseph and Mary came together. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18 and 1:20, with [L2] *ek* (out of, source) and *gennaō* (to beget).
2. Mary was a virgin who had known no man, and the angel's answer to "how" names the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, not a man. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:34-35, with [L2] *ginōskō* (to know), *episkiazō* (to overshadow), and [L3] Matthew 1:25.
3. The prophecy points to the woman's seed and a virgin who conceives, and Matthew applies it to this conception. Footing: [L1] Isaiah 7:14 and Matthew 1:23, with [L2] *almah* (the Hebrew behind KJV "virgin") and [L3] Genesis 3:15.
4. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern at Joseph, and Luke calls Joseph's fatherhood "supposed." Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16 and Luke 3:23, with [L2] feminine *hēs* (of whom) and *nomizō* (to suppose).
5. The body was prepared by God and the Son was made of a woman, with no human father named. Footing: [L1] Hebrews 10:5 and Galatians 4:4, with [L2] *katartizō* (to prepare) and *ek gynaikos* (out of a woman).
6. Christ had no human biological father; Joseph was his legal and household father only. Footing: [L4] chain from links 1-5, resting on [L1] Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35 and [L2] *ek* (out of, source) and *dio* (therefore).

=== [CR2] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# Defender, Round 2: Link Round and Answer to the Closing Question

**Position held.** [L4] Christ had no human biological father. The Holy Ghost is the source of the conception. Joseph is the husband who took Mary and the legal head of the house in which the child was reckoned. The seed of David and of Judah comes to Christ through Mary.

## The closing question: Hebrews 7:14 and "the house of their fathers"

[L1] Hebrews 7:14: "For [it is] evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood."

[L2] The word behind "sprang" is *anatellō* (G393, "to arise, to rise as the sun"). The thing the verse calls "evident" is the arising "out of Juda," a tribe.

[L3] Luke 3:31 gives Mary's line to the tribe: "which was [the son] of Nathan, which was [the son] of David." Luke 3:23 sets that line beside "Heli" and calls Joseph's sonship "supposed."

[L4] The tribe is the content of Hebrews 7:14, and Luke 3:23 and 3:31 supply a line from Judah's David to Christ that runs apart from Joseph's father Jacob (Matthew 1:16). That meets the verse.

[L1] Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers."

[L3] Luke 2:4: Joseph "was of the house and lineage of David." Luke 2:5: "To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child."

[L4] Luke 2:5 states that Mary was taxed with Joseph, and Luke 2:4 states that Joseph was of David's house. The register reckons the household under the house of the husband, which is the "house of the fathers" rule applied to the taxing. The rule fixes the household's register, and the flesh through Mary meets "sprang out of Juda."

[L1] Ezra 2:62: "These sought their register [among] those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."

[L4] Ezra 2:62 states the ground of the exclusion: "they were not found" in the register, and the word "therefore" carries that cause. Ezra 2:61 states that they "took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name." The stated ground is the missing register. The child in Luke 2:4-5 stands in the register of Joseph's house, so Ezra 2:59-62 does not bar him.

## LINK ROUND

### LINK 1: SUPPORTED

**Pressed witnesses, quoted.**
- [L1] Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
- [L1] 1 John 5:1: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God."
- [L1] John 1:13: "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
- [L1] John 3:6: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
- [L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
- [L1] Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband, being a just [man]... was minded to put her away privily."
- [L1] Matthew 1:24: "took unto him his wife."
- [L1] Deuteronomy 20:7: "that hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her."
- [L1] Deuteronomy 22:24: "the man, because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife."

**Answer to the *ek* and *gennaō* press (1 John 5:1, John 1:13, John 3:6).**

[L2] *Ek* (G1537, "out of," source) with *gennaō* (G1080, "to beget, to be born") stands in John 1:13 as *ek theou* (out of God). The verse sets it against three other sources: "blood" (*haima*, G129), "the will of the flesh" (*sarx*, G4561) and "the will of man" (*anēr*, G435).

[L4] John 1:13 makes "of God" a source set over against blood and the will of man. John 3:6 sorts begetting into two kinds, "of the flesh" and "of the Spirit." Matthew 1:20 files the thing conceived in Mary under the second kind: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." A fleshly begetting by Joseph would belong to the first kind, and the row states the other.

[L4] Believers in 1 John 5:1 are already born of flesh when they are "born of God." That is a second birth added to a first. In Matthew 1:20 the Spirit is the stated source of the one conception in Mary's womb ("that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost"), and the same verse gives it as the reason for Joseph to receive her.

**Answer to the "fear not" and "put her away" press (Matthew 1:19-20).**

[L1] Matthew 1:20 gives a reason: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: *for* that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

[L2] *Phobeō* (G5399, "to be afraid") names his fear. *Gar* (G1063, "for") gives the cause that ends it.

[L3] Matthew 1:19 shows what that fear was: Joseph was "minded to put her away privily," and was "not willing to make her a publick example." The "publick example" is the penalty of Deuteronomy 22:24: "ye shall stone them with stones that they die," for "the man, because he hath humbled his neighbour's wife." The challenger's own witness describes the sin Joseph feared. Joseph is called "a just [man]."

[L4] A husband who knew himself the father would have had no cause to put her away privily. Joseph's purpose in Matthew 1:19 and the reason given in Matthew 1:20 both show the Holy Ghost, and not the husband, as the source of the conception.

**Answer to the "came together" press (Matthew 1:24, Deuteronomy 20:7).**

[L3] Deuteronomy 20:7 describes the betrothed man as one who "hath not taken her." Matthew 1:24 records the taking: "took unto him his wife." Both rows place the taking after the espousal. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together," which is before the taking of 1:24.

[L3] Luke 1:27 and Luke 1:34 show Mary at the angel's word. She is "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph," and she says "I know not a man."

[L4] On the challenger's own reading, Luke 1:34 states her condition at that moment, and the moment lies within the espousal. Her stated condition within the espousal is that she knew "not a man." That answers the step from "husband and wife by espousal" to "union within the espousal."

### LINK 2: SUPPORTED

**Pressed witnesses, quoted.**
- [L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- [L1] Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb."
- [L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L1] Acts 1:8: "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you."
- [L1] Luke 9:34: "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them."
- [L1] Acts 5:15: "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them."
- [L1] Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain."
- [L1] Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
- [L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

**Answer to the tense press (Luke 1:34 with Luke 1:31).**

[L4] The challenger says "I know not" (*ginōskō*, G1097, "to know") is present and the conception is future. I grant both, and both support my link. Luke 1:31 puts the conception after her words, and the angel's reply, "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee" (*eperchomai*, G1904, "to come upon"), is also future. So the conception follows a moment when she is a virgin who knows "not a man," and the angel's reply gives the means.

**Answer to the *eperchomai* and *episkiazō* press (Acts 1:8, Luke 9:34, Acts 5:15).**

[L2] The Holy Ghost "come upon" gives power in Acts 1:8. *Episkiazō* (G1982, "to overshadow") is a presence resting upon someone in Luke 9:34 and Acts 5:15. I grant both senses.

[L4] The question in Luke 1:34 is "How shall this be?" The answer in Luke 1:35 is the Holy Ghost's coming and the Highest's power overshadowing. A power and presence given as the answer to "how" is the means of the conception. If Joseph were the means, the angel's reply would stand in the wrong place in the exchange.

**Answer to the "therefore also" press (Luke 1:32).**

[L2] *Dio* (G1352, "wherefore, for which reason") joins the last clause of Luke 1:35 to the clause before it. *Kaleō* (G2564, "to call") gives the title.

[L1] Luke 1:35: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

[L4] The reason given for the title "Son of God" is in the same sentence: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." The title rests on that cause.

[L3] Hebrews 7:9: "Levi also, who receiveth tithes, payed tithes in Abraham." Hebrews 7:10: "he was yet in the loins of his father." Here "father" is used of Abraham, an ancestor of Levi three generations back.

[L4] Luke 1:32's "his father David" is the same ancestral use. It states David as the forefather from whom the throne comes to a descendant.

**Answer to the Genesis 4:1 and "till" press (Matthew 1:25).**

[L1] Genesis 4:1: "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived." That is the stated means of an ordinary begetting, and it uses *yāda‘* (H3045, "to know") of a husband.

[L2] Luke 1:34 uses the same sense of knowing, *ginōskō*, and Mary says "I know not a man." Matthew 1:25 uses *ginōskō* for Joseph: "knew her not till she had brought forth." *Heōs* (G2193, "until") sets the limit at the birth.

[L3] Matthew 1:24 puts the taking first: "took unto him his wife," and then "knew her not."

[L4] From the taking to the birth, Matthew 1:25 states "knew her not." Before the taking, the espoused Mary says "I know not a man" (Luke 1:34). [VOID (pkgBAR): a barred move struck by the system. The press this answered counts as unanswered.]

### LINK 3: SUPPORTED, narrowed

**Pressed witnesses, quoted.**
- [L1] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed."
- [L1] Genesis 4:25: "Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son... hath appointed me another seed instead of Abel."
- [L1] Genesis 16:10: "I will multiply thy seed exceedingly."
- [L1] Genesis 16:15: "And Hagar bare Abram a son."
- [L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
- [L1] Isaiah 7:16: "before the child shall know to refuse the evil, and choose the good."
- [L1] Isaiah 8:3-4: "I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son... before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother."
- [L1] Isaiah 8:8: "thy land, O Immanuel."
- [L1] Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David."

**Concession and narrowing.** [L4] Genesis 4:25 says Eve's seed Seth came after "Adam knew his wife again," and Genesis 16:15 says "Hagar bare Abram a son" while Genesis 16:10 calls the same line her "seed." So in Genesis 3:15 "her seed" is a word for a woman's offspring in general, and I do not rest the exclusion of a father on it. The kept link is the sign of Isaiah 7:14, which Matthew 1:22-23 applies to Mary: a virgin conceiving.

**Answer on Isaiah 7:14.**

[L1] Isaiah 7:11: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above."

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive."

[L2] *'Ôth* (H226, "sign") is the word in both verses.

[L4] The sign is offered from "the depth" or "the height above," and Isaiah 7:14 says "the Lord himself shall give you a sign." A sign the Lord himself gives from such a range is a wonder, and an ordinary conception by a husband's approach is not that kind of sign. Isaiah 8:3 sets the ordinary event in different words: "I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived." That row says "the prophetess" and "I went unto," where Isaiah 7:14 says "a virgin shall conceive." Isaiah 7:16's "before the child shall know" gives the time-limit of the political sign alongside the virgin.

[L1] Matthew 1:22: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet," followed in Matthew 1:23 by "Behold, a virgin shall be with child."

[L2] *Parthenos* (G3933, "virgin") is the word in Matthew 1:23 and in Luke 1:27.

[L4] Luke 1:27 joins the virgin to an espousal to Joseph. Luke 1:34 puts her still a virgin who says "I know not a man." Matthew 1:22-23 says "all this was done" to fulfil the virgin's sign. The kept link stands on Isaiah 7:11, 7:14, Matthew 1:22-23, Luke 1:27 and Luke 1:34.

### LINK 4: SUPPORTED

**Pressed witnesses, quoted.**
- [L1] Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."
- [L1] Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."
- [L1] Luke 2:7: "she brought forth her firstborn son."
- [L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- [L1] Acts 16:13: "where prayer was wont to be made."
- [L1] Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled."
- [L1] Luke 2:41: "his parents went to Jerusalem every year."
- [L1] Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
- [L1] 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son... I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."

**Answer on Matthew 1:16 against Luke 1:13.**

[L1] Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob."

[L2] *Gennaō* (G1080) is active ("begat") in each row up to Jacob and Joseph. In the last clause *egennēthē* (was born) is passive, and *hēs* (of whom) is feminine singular, pointing to Mary.

[L4] Luke 1:13 reads "shall bear *thee* a son," so the father is joined to the birth in that clause. Matthew 1:16 states "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus": the relation it gives for Joseph is "husband," and the birth is "of whom," feminine. The two rows differ in what they state, and Matthew 1:18-20 supplies the account of the birth.

**Answer on *nomizō* (Luke 3:23, Acts 16:13).**

[L2] *Nomizō* (G3543, "to deem by custom, to suppose") stands in both verses. In Acts 16:13 it is a custom held, as "was wont," where the party went out expecting a place of prayer. I grant it can carry custom.

[L4] In Luke 3:23 the narrator sets the clause in a parenthesis, "(as was supposed)." The parenthesis marks the common estimate and holds the narrator's own voice apart from it. The same writer reports the cause of the sonship in Luke 1:35: "therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." John 6:42 shows the crowd's side: "the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know." The crowd's knowledge in that row is what Luke 3:23 marks as "supposed."

**Answer on Luke 2:33, 2:41, 2:48-49.**

[L1] Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled."

[L4] Speaking in his own voice about the child with the two of them, the narrator writes "Joseph and his mother," each by a different relation. In Luke 2:41 "his parents" is the household that went up. In Luke 2:48 Mary says "thy father and I." In Luke 2:49 the child answers in the same exchange: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Mary says "thy father," and the answer sets "my Father" over against it. 1 Chronicles 28:6 gives God's fatherhood by choice: "I have chosen him [to be] my son." Luke 1:35 gives the sonship by the Holy Ghost's coming, "therefore also." That is a cause, where 1 Chronicles 28:6 states a choice among sons.

### LINK 5: SUPPORTED, narrowed

**Pressed witnesses, quoted.**
- [L1] Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman, made under the law."
- [L1] Job 14:1: "Man [that is] born of a woman [is] of few days."
- [L1] Matthew 11:11: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist."
- [L1] Hebrews 2:14: "he also himself likewise took part of the same."
- [L1] Hebrews 2:16: "he took on [him] the seed of Abraham."
- [L1] Hebrews 2:17: "in all things it behoved him to be made like unto [his] brethren."

**Concession.** [L4] "Of a woman" in Job 14:1 and Matthew 11:11 is said of men who had fathers (Luke 1:13 gives John's father Zacharias). I grant that Galatians 4:4 alone is a phrase of mortal birth, so the link is narrowed to the paired verb in Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4 and to Hebrews 10:5.

**Answer.**

[L2] *Ginomai* (G1096, "to become, be made") is the verb in Galatians 4:4, "made of a woman," and in Romans 1:3, "made of the seed of David."

[L4] The same verb is used in both rows of the same person. If "made of the seed of David" and "made of a woman" are two parts of one making, then the seed of David was made through the woman. This is developed under LINK 6.

[L1] Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me." The margin reads "thou hast fitted me."

[L2] *Katartizō* (G2675, "to fit, to prepare") has God as the one who prepares: "thou hast fitted me."

**Answer on Hebrews 2:14-17.**

[L1] Hebrews 2:14 states the likeness: "the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same." The thing shared is "flesh and blood."

[L3] Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee." The thing born is "of thee," from Mary, and flesh and blood come from her.

[L4] Hebrews 2:17 says "in all things... like unto [his] brethren," and Hebrews 2:14 gives the respect as "flesh and blood." Both are met by the flesh from Mary, which Luke 1:35 states as "born of thee."

### LINK 6 (keystone): SUPPORTED

**Pressed witnesses, quoted.**
- [L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- [L1] Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne."
- [L1] Hebrews 7:10: "he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him."
- [L1] 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."
- [L1] Psalms 132:11: "Of the fruit of thy body will I set upon thy throne."
- [L1] Hebrews 7:14: "our Lord sprang out of Juda."
